name: V-neck sweater vest

image.caption: Mr Awkward Mitten Pockets Ugly Christmas Sweater Vest

lead: A V-neck sweater vest is a sleeveless knitted garment worn over a collared shirt, a layering piece that has moved in and out of fashion for over a century. Its low V neckline shows the shirt collar and tie, which draws the eye to the face and upper chest.

People use it as a style tool: it adds a layer of texture without bulk in the arms, can make a torso look more structured, and gives a preppy or vintage look. Reference sources describe it as popular in the 20th century, particularly the 1970s in the UK, and as returning to popularity in the 21st century.

paras: It is worn over a button-up shirt, sometimes with a tie, in cable knit, argyle, fair isle or plain knits. Fit matters: a closer, shorter cut defines the waist, while a looser one reads more casual. It is combined with chinos, tailored trousers or jeans depending on the look wanted.
There are no health risks. The look can read as dated or costume-like for some wearers, and thick knits can add visual bulk to the torso.

angle.text: Worn over a shirt, the vest adds a textured layer that draws the eye up to the chest and face. A well-fitted one can give the torso shape while keeping arms slim.

lead: A sweater vest is a sleeveless knit pullover, similar to a sweater but usually with a low-cut neckline, known in the UK as a slipover or sleeveless jumper and historically in Commonwealth countries as a spencer [1]. The V-neck version is the most common form.

As a style choice it works by layering: the V frames the shirt collar, adds color and texture to the chest and, because it has no sleeves, lets the shirt cuffs and arms stay slim. Wearers use it to add structure to the torso and to move an outfit toward a preppy, academic or retro aesthetic.

Wikipedia notes the garment was popular in the 20th century, particularly in the 1970s in the UK, and has grown in popularity again in the 21st century [1]. Grokipedia traces the term to around 1903 and golf wear, and mentions argyle and fair isle patterns, the Prince of Wales vest of the 1920s and 1930s, and wearers such as Woodrow Wilson and Herbert Hoover [2].

paras: Grokipedia describes the garment as a sleeveless knit covering the torso from shoulders to waist, worn for added warmth and formality without restricting arm movement, in pullover or button-front varieties with textures such as cable knits or ribbing [2]. Cable-knit versions are typically worn by cricketers, and golfers and sports fans commonly wear them, including vests with NFL and college team logos [1].

Grokipedia dates the term to about 1903 and describes early designs rooted in 19th-century golf attire, entering mainstream menswear in the 1910s and becoming a staple in the 1920s and 1930s [2]. Wikipedia describes 1970s UK popularity and a 21st-century revival [1]. In 2012 Rick Santorum's sweater vest attracted media attention, and coach Jim Tressel earned the nickname The Sweater Vest [1].

Forum mentions of sweater vests are usually passing comments about fashion types, from jokes about a vintage, tight sweater vest in the context of a hipster look [3] to descriptions of a preppy or museum-going style [4]. The garment appears in style discussions as an example of the layered knit trend.

timeline.event: The term sweater vest first appears in English, per Grokipedia [2].
Patterned vests such as the Prince of Wales style become a menswear staple [2].
Rick Santorum's vest becomes a media talking point [1].
